composition.story: Merge sort sorts eight numbers by halving them until each run holds one item, then merging sorted runs back up. Step through splits and merges; watch the comparison counter. The final state shows every merge level touches all eight items once across log₂8 = 3 levels, so total work is n·log₂n — here 17 comparisons, exactly the worst-case bound.

aha.observation: Each of the three merge levels touches all 8 items once, so the total is about n·log₂n. These 17 comparisons equal the worst-case bound n⌈log₂n⌉−2^⌈log₂n⌉+1.

parts.presentation: Top row above the picture, with short step labels. The status line below shows state.sentence. The rail also serves as the progress trace.
Recursion tree drawn as array-cell rows: split rows go down, then merge rows go back up. Active rows are highlighted and links show split/merge arrows.
Faint outline of the rows that were active in the previous step.
Anchored to the active row. It says where the work happens; counts appear only in the readouts.
Panel under the picture: comparisons in this step, running total, merge levels done, and the fixed worst-case bound for n=8.

controls.label: Step
controls.presentation: Previous and Next buttons keep their names when disabled at either end. Left and Right arrow keys also work, with visible focus. States 1–9 are logical steps, not clock time.

controls.label: Reset to first step
controls.presentation: Returns to s1-start. The input is fixed at 38 27 43 3 9 82 10 5, so there is no parameter control.

states.label: Start
states.sentence: Merge sort begins with eight unsorted numbers. It will split them down, then merge sorted runs back up.

states.label: Split halves
states.sentence: Cut the array into a left half and a right half. Splitting only picks a midpoint and compares nothing.
states.why: The midpoint index is n/2; values are not inspected.

states.label: Split quarters
states.sentence: Halve each run again. Every halving adds one level to the tree.

states.label: Single items
states.sentence: Every run now holds one item, and a single item is already sorted. Halving eight down to one took log₂8 levels.
states.why: Base case: a run of length 1 needs no work.

states.label: Merge pairs
states.sentence: Merge neighbouring singles. One comparison per pair puts the smaller item first.
states.why: Merging two runs of length 1 needs at most 1 comparison.

states.label: Merge left
states.sentence: Compare the two front items and move the smaller one out: 3, then 27, then 38. Then 43 copies over.
states.why: Merging runs of length a and b needs at most a+b−1 comparisons.

states.label: Merge right
states.sentence: Same rule on the right side: 5, 9 and 10 leave by comparison. Then 82 copies over without one.
states.why: Once one run empties, the rest copies with no comparisons.

states.label: Final merge
states.sentence: Final merge: 3, 5, 9 and 10 have left the runs. The left front, 27, now waits against 82.
states.why: Each comparison moves exactly one item to the output.

states.label: Sorted
states.sentence: Sorted. Each merge level touched all eight items once, and halving made three levels, so the work is about n·log₂n.
states.why: Per level ≤ n−1 comparisons, times log₂n levels; this input hits the bound.

1.reason: The recursion-tree rows with split and merge links answer why merge sort costs n·log₂n, via 3 levels each touching all 8 items.

2.reason: The aha state s9-final is the last step; stepping is user-driven (not timed), so it holds there with the sorted row active and 17=17 shown.

3.reason: The only control is the step index, which changes the active rows and readouts; the fixed input is explicitly justified as no parameter.

4.reason: Highlights come from state.active, the ghost from previous.active, the callout from calloutRegion/short/why, and the readouts from state.readouts, all declared in the data.

6.reason: The narrative, step labels, region labels and readouts consistently name the same splits, merges, runs and levels.

7.reason: Detailed depth adds the merge-by-merge comparison counts and the bound formula, and only the active rows are highlighted at a time, so the density stays tolerable.
